st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: The supplied excerpts are bibliography entries only. Although the cited topics overlap with the cluster’s focus on augmentation, organisational learning, teamwork and coordination, they do not reveal the source’s own findings or stance on whether AI redistributes legal tasks, status and professional power.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Provides concrete field-experimental evidence that GenAI can improve bounded knowledge-work performance and reconfigure collaboration, while reinforcing the cluster’s caution that sustained effects on expertise development and transfer remain unresolved. It extends the cluster’s organisational-complements argument, though it is not direct evidence about legal workflows or verification.
qs: Individuals working with AI showed a substantial 0.37 standard deviation performance increase over the baseline of working alone without AI.

Future research should examine how these patterns evolve as users develop greater AI proficiency, how different organizational contexts moderate these effects, and how sustained AI use impacts the development and transfer of expertise within organizations.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s productivity effects depend on task and workflow configuration, and materially extends the cluster with randomized workplace evidence: AI-assisted individuals can substitute for some collaborative functions on average, while human–AI teams retain an advantage for exceptional outputs. Its short-duration, cross-functional design also limits claims about persistent or general productivity gains.
qs: Our findings reveal that AI significantly enhances performance: individuals with AI matched the performance of teams without AI, demonstrating that AI can effectively replicate certain benefits of human collaboration.

At the same time, an important nuance emerges when considering top-tier solutions: AI-augmented teams were more likely to produce proposals ranking in the top decile, underscoring the unique synergy produced by combining human collaboration with AI-based augmentation.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The study supports selective, human-led deployment and materially extends the cluster with field-experimental evidence that AI can improve quality and speed, bridge functional expertise and alter optimal team design. Its structured intervention, heterogeneous user practices and explicit limits on generalisability reinforce the importance of interaction design and operating-model redesign rather than autonomous substitution.
qs: Our intent was not to automate any part of the existing workflow but rather to help participants engage in their standard exploratory process, using the AI as they saw fit.

Some firms may focus on the efficiency side, while others may focus on the complementarity.16 The increased speed and comprehensiveness of AI-enabled work—evidenced by significantly longer solutions produced in less time—suggests opportunities to redesign work processes and deliverable expectations.

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between assisted task performance and broader career outcomes. It provides randomized evidence of performance gains and substitution for some collaborative functions, while making no claim that these gains improve employment, income or long-term expertise.
qs: Individuals working with AI showed a substantial 0.37 standard deviation performance increase over the baseline of working alone without AI.

This finding suggests that AI can effectively substitute for certain collaborative functions, acting as a genuine teammate by granting individuals access to the varied expertise and perspectives traditionally provided by team members.

st.t: Assisted performance: Gains vary by skill measure
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between measured quality gains and broader claims of uniform improvement or worker substitution. AI-assisted individuals and teams outperform the reference group on standardized solution quality, but direct comparisons do not establish that AI-assisted teams outperform unaided teams on average quality or top-decile outcomes at the 5% level. The evidence is task- and outcome-specific and does not demonstrate substitution.

st.t: Creative diversity: Individual gains can homogenise groups
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal distinction: AI assistance improved individual and team performance while also increasing semantic similarity across outputs. Its retention analysis further supports the cluster’s qualification that extensive AI-text use does not by itself establish passive copying, because humans continued to shape and contextualize outputs.
qs: Individuals working with AI showed a substantial 0.37 standard deviation performance increase over the baseline of working alone without AI.
While human-only solutions (both individual and pair) show relatively dispersed distributions, AI-aided solutions demonstrate notably higher semantic similarity.

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between AI-assisted performance gains and wholesale human replacement. Its randomized field experiment finds improved performance for AI-assisted individuals, while the semantic analysis indicates that participants meaningfully shaped and contextualized AI outputs. It does not provide evidence about durable skill formation or whole-job productivity.
qs: Individuals working with AI showed a substantial 0.37 standard deviation performance increase over the baseline of working alone without AI.

This finding becomes particularly interesting when considered alongside our retention analysis: despite the high retention rates of AI-generated content in final solutions, the semantic fingerprint of AI-aided solutions remains closer to human-only solutions than to pure AI outputs, indicating that humans meaningfully shape and contextualize AI suggestions rather than merely adopting them wholesale.

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s insistence on evaluating AI through controlled comparisons and distinct practical outcomes rather than inferring productivity from adoption or capability. Its randomized four-condition design separates AI assistance from human teamwork, while measuring time, expected quality, expertise deployment and emotional experience separately. However, the supplied evidence does not reveal the direction or magnitude of the main effects, so it supports the cluster’s methodological proposition rather than establishing productivity gains.
qs: the four conditions were: (1) Control: Individual without AI, (2) Treatment 1 (T1): Team (R&D + Commercial) without AI, (3) Treatment 2 (T2): Individual + AI, and (4) Treatment 3 (T3): Team (R&D + Commercial) + AI.
Expected Quality is a binary variable based on survey responses, where participants indicated whether they expected their solution to rank in the top 10% (1) or not (0).

kp.k: Randomized experiment tests AI in consumer-product innovation
kp.d: The authors report a pre-registered field experiment conducted at Procter & Gamble between May and July 2024. The principal analysis covers 776 professionals assigned to work individually or in Commercial–R&D pairs, with or without AI, on real early-stage innovation challenges. AI participants received one hour of training and used GPT-4 through Microsoft Azure; July participants had GPT-4o. This is evidence about consumer-product knowledge work, not a direct study of legal services.
qs: Between May and July 2024, we conducted a large-scale field experiment at Procter & Gamble (P&G) to evaluate how GenAI influences cross-functional new product development.
Our analyses focus on 776 of these participants who were randomly assigned across four conditions.
Participants at the July workshop had access to GPT-4o.

kp.k: AI-assisted individuals matched unaided teams on average quality
kp.d: Relative to individuals without AI, the reported average quality improvements were 0.24 standard deviations for teams without AI (p < 0.05), 0.37 for individuals with AI (p < 0.01), and 0.39 for teams with AI (p < 0.01). The authors interpret the comparable performance of AI-assisted individuals and unaided pairs as substitution for certain collaborative functions. AI-assisted teams did not significantly outperform AI-assisted individuals; Table 2 also reports no statistically significant team-with-AI versus team-without-AI difference.
qs: Teams without AI show a quality improvement of 0.24 standard deviations over individuals without AI (p < 0.05), highlighting the traditional benefits of collaboration.
The impact of AI is more substantial: individuals with AI demonstrate a 0.37 standard deviation increase (p < 0.01), while teams with AI show a 0.39 standard deviation improvement (p < 0.01).
their performance was not significantly different from that of individuals using AI.

kp.k: AI reduced task time and expanded submissions
kp.d: The results narrative reports 16.4% less task time for AI-assisted individuals and 12.7% less for AI-assisted teams relative to unaided individuals. Table 3's first specification reports submissions longer by 504.507 and 543.745 words, respectively, against a control mean of 381.422 words. These are measures of task duration and output length, rather than evidence of implemented innovation or commercial returns.
qs: individuals with AI spent 16.4% less time than the control group, while teams with AI spent 12.7% less time.
While teams without AI produced solutions only marginally longer than individual controls, the introduction of AI led to substantially longer outputs.

kp.k: AI helped employees bridge task-experience gaps
kp.d: The authors distinguish employees whose core responsibilities include product development from those less frequently involved in it. They report that AI-assisted non-core employees working alone reached quality levels comparable to teams containing at least one core employee, interpreting this as access to expertise otherwise supplied through collaboration or supervision. The paper leaves open whether such assistance develops enduring expertise.
qs: However, when given access to AI, non-core-job employees working alone achieved performance levels comparable to teams with at least one core-job employee.
AI allows less experienced employees to achieve performance levels that previously required either direct collaboration or supervision by colleagues with more task-related experience.
Does AI-enabled boundary spanning lead to genuine expertise development, or does it primarily facilitate access to existing knowledge?

kp.k: AI broadened solutions beyond participants’ functional specialisms
kp.d: Unaided R&D professionals tended toward technical proposals and Commercial professionals toward commercial ones. With AI, their solution-orientation distributions became more alike, without a significant relationship between technical orientation and quality. AI-enabled pairs also showed a shift from bimodality (0.564) toward unimodality (0.482). The authors interpret this distributional pattern as potentially reducing dominance by one functional perspective, rather than directly demonstrating equal participation.
qs: Without AI assistance, participants tended to generate ideas closely aligned with their professional backgrounds.
Both commercial and technical participants generated a more balanced mix of ideas, spanning the commercial/technical spectrum.
Moreover, quality scores did not significantly vary based on a solution’s technical orientation, indicating that these effects did not come at the cost of solution effectiveness.
This shift from bimodality to unimodality, while preserving the range of technical depth, suggests that AI helps reduce dominance effects in team collaboration.

kp.k: AI teams increased top-decile outcomes against individual controls
kp.d: In an additional analysis, teams with AI were 9.2 percentage points more likely than unaided individuals to produce a top-decile solution, against a 5.8% control mean. The authors describe this as around three times the chance. Table 10 shows that the individual-with-AI effect was not statistically significant; direct comparisons of AI teams with unaided teams (p = 0.190) or AI individuals (p = 0.061) were not significant at 5% in the first specification. The authors nevertheless suggest human–AI complementarity may matter particularly for exceptional ideas.
qs: teams with AI were 9.2 percentage points more likely to produce solutions in the top decile compared to the control mean of 5.8%, that corresponds to around 3 times more chances of being in the top decile of solutions.
this effect is not statistically significant, suggesting that the combination of AI and teamwork might be particularly powerful for achieving exceptional performance.

kp.d: Against unaided individuals, AI-assisted individuals and teams reported positive-emotion increases of 0.457 and 0.635 standard deviations, respectively (p < 0.01), and negative-emotion decreases of 0.233 and 0.235 standard deviations (p < 0.05) in the initial specification. Table 7 shows the team negative-emotion effect was not statistically significant with full controls. Sociality was operationalized through short-term self-reported emotions, and the authors qualify the claim that AI substitutes for some social benefits of teamwork.
qs: Specifically, individuals with AI showed a 0.457 standard deviation increase in positive emotions (p < 0.01) compared to the control group, while teams with AI demonstrated an even larger 0.635 standard deviation increase (p < 0.01).

While AI cannot fully replicate the richness of human social and emotional interaction, its ability to contribute as a genuine collaborator suggests a marked shift in how knowledge work can be structured and carried out.

kp.k: Better performance did not translate into greater confidence
kp.d: The authors report that AI-enabled participants were 9.2 percentage points less likely to expect a top-10% ranking than controls (p < 0.05), despite better objectively rated performance. Separately, increased expected future AI use correlated with more positive and fewer negative emotions; the authors explicitly caution that this association does not establish causality.
qs: AI-enabled participants were 9.2 percentage points less likely to expect their solutions to rank in the top 10% compared to the control group (p < 0.05), suggesting a disconnect between actual and perceived performance.
While this correlation cannot definitely establish causality, it suggests an interesting relationship between positive experiences with AI and anticipated future engagement with the technology.

kp.k: High AI-content retention coexisted with iterative human involvement
kp.d: The retention measure identified final-submission sentences matching AI-generated sentences at least 90%, excluding initial human prompts. Many submissions had high AI-content retention, while others retained none and used AI for ideation or validation. Participants retaining some AI content averaged 18.7 prompts; those with entirely AI-generated submission content averaged 23.9. The authors caution that retention is not sufficient evidence of passive copying. Their prompting approach deliberately elicited human judgment rather than automating the workflow.
qs: However, high retention rates do not necessarily indicate passive AI adoption—participants may engage extensively with the tool through iterative prompting, validation of responses, critical evaluation, and incorporation of domain expertise in their prompting strategy.
Notably, participants whose solutions showed 100% AI-generated content averaged 23.9 prompts, suggesting extensive iterative interaction with the tool rather than simple copy-and-paste behavior.
Our intent was not to automate any part of the existing workflow but rather to help participants engage in their standard exploratory process, using the AI as they saw fit.

kp.k: AI assistance increased similarity without eliminating human influence
kp.d: Semantic analysis found greater similarity among AI-assisted submissions than among human-only submissions. An additional AI-only comparison clustered more tightly still. The authors interpret the AI-assisted solutions’ relative proximity to human-only solutions as evidence that participants shaped and contextualized model output, even when retaining substantial generated text.
qs: While human-only solutions (both individual and pair) show relatively dispersed distributions, AI-aided solutions demonstrate notably higher semantic similarity.

despite the high retention rates of AI-generated content in final solutions, the semantic fingerprint of AI-aided solutions remains closer to human-only solutions than to pure AI outputs, indicating that humans meaningfully shape and contextualize AI suggestions rather than merely adopting them wholesale.

kp.k: Authors recommend reconsidering team design and AI training
kp.d: The authors propose that organizations reconsider team size, composition, processes and deliverable expectations, balancing individual efficiency with possible team complementarity for exceptional outcomes. They recommend developing AI-interaction skills and broader cross-functional thinking. Predictions that experience and purpose-built collaborative tools could increase benefits are prospective, not experimentally established results.
qs: First, organizations may need to fundamentally rethink optimal team sizes and compositions.
Some firms may focus on the efficiency side, while others may focus on the complementarity.
Organizations should invest in developing their workers’ AI interaction capabilities, as this appears to be an increasingly critical skill.
Purpose-built collaborative AI systems could potentially unlock significantly greater benefits by better supporting group dynamics and collective problem-solving processes.

kp.k: Short-duration design and subjective evaluation limit conclusions
kp.d: The April 2025 paper is a working paper, not peer-reviewed. Its one-day virtual collaborations involved cross-functional pairs rather than sustained work or larger teams. Quality was assessed blind to condition; the appendix reports 22 evaluators, 1,595 evaluations of 550 solutions, 2.89 assessments per solution, and ICC2 reliability of 0.452. The authors acknowledge uncertainty about longer-term skill development, trust and transfer to other organizational contexts.
qs: They have not been peer-reviewed or been subject to the review by the NBER Board of Directors that accompanies official NBER publications.
our experiment relied on one-day virtual collaborations that did not fully capture the day-to-day complexities of team interactions in organizations
collaborations involving team members with similar expertise, or in larger, more intricate team structures, may exhibit different patterns of AI adoption and effectiveness.
Evaluators were blind to experimental conditions and used predefined metrics.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Dell’Acqua and co-authors claim that generative AI can reproduce some benefits of human teamwork in product innovation: improving individual performance, spanning functional expertise and improving reported emotional experience. They also identify potential complementarity between AI and human teams for exceptional outcomes.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of consumer packaged goods innovation, not legal services. The authors report quality improvements relative to individuals without AI of approximately 0.24 standard deviations for teams without AI, 0.37 for individuals with AI and 0.39 for teams with AI. They interpret the comparable performance of AI-assisted individuals and unassisted pairs as substitution for certain collaborative functions, not replacement of human workers generally. They report task-time reductions of 16.4% for AI-assisted individuals and 12.7% for AI-assisted teams, alongside substantially longer submissions. AI assistance reduced differences between technically oriented R&D proposals and commercially oriented Commercial proposals. Employees for whom product development was not a core responsibility could, with AI, reach performance comparable to teams containing a core-job employee. AI users also reported more positive and fewer negative emotions. In additional analyses, AI-assisted teams were 9.2 percentage points more likely than the individual-without-AI baseline of 5.8% to produce top-decile solutions; the individual-with-AI increase was not statistically significant. The authors suggest that organizations may consequently redesign team size, composition and workflows, choosing between efficiency and human–AI complementarity. They also find greater semantic similarity among AI-assisted submissions, while interpreting their difference from AI-only outputs as evidence that humans meaningfully shaped the results.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The central claims rest on a preregistered randomized field experiment, with blinded assessment of proposals, task-duration records, surveys and analyses of AI interactions and submitted text.
pts.d: The authors describe an analysis of 776 randomly assigned P&G professionals in four conditions: individual without AI, cross-functional pair without AI, individual with AI and cross-functional pair with AI. Participants addressed real business-unit innovation challenges. Main comparisons use initial between-subject outcomes, before control participants received AI training and repeated the task. Appendix B reports 22 evaluators conducting 1,595 assessments across 550 solutions, averaging 2.89 assessments per solution; evaluators were experienced professionals who were MBA or Engineering students or recent graduates. Quality, novelty, feasibility and related dimensions were rated, with quality standardized against individual controls. Regression specifications add business-unit/date fixed effects and participant controls. The positive-emotion estimates are 0.457 standard deviations for AI-assisted individuals and 0.635 for AI-assisted teams; negative-emotion estimates are −0.233 and −0.235 in the baseline specification, although the team negative-emotion effect is not statistically significant with full controls. Top-decile gains for AI-assisted teams are statistically significant against individual controls, but Table 10 does not show significance at 5% against either unassisted teams or AI-assisted individuals. The organizational-design implications and possible future gains are interpretations rather than observed restructuring outcomes. The paper is a working paper not yet peer-reviewed. The supplied text contains reporting differences that should remain distinct: Table 1 totals 791 participants rather than the stated 776, and Table 4's log-time coefficients differ from the narrative percentage reductions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The demonstrated effects are immediate workshop outcomes from May–July 2024; broader organizational changes and stronger future benefits are conditional possibilities without a specified implementation horizon.
pts.d: The April 2025 working paper reports one-day virtual workshops involving early-stage product innovation. Participants worked within their own business units, individually or in pairs comprising one Commercial and one R&D professional. AI conditions received one hour of training and recommended prompts. The tool used GPT-4 through Microsoft Azure, with GPT-4o available in the July workshop. The authors qualify generalization to sustained workplace collaboration, larger teams and teams with similar expertise. They suggest that inexperienced prompting and tools not optimized for collaboration may mean observed benefits are a lower bound, but do not demonstrate those future improvements. Emotional outcomes concern short-term self-reports rather than the full richness of human social connection. Long-term expertise development, learning and trust remain open questions. The intervention was designed to support human exploration and iterative judgment, not autonomously replace the workflow.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are experienced Commercial and R&D professionals at P&G, especially employees less familiar with product development, and managers designing innovation teams.
pts.d: Participants came from Baby Care, Feminine Care, Grooming and Oral Care in Europe and the Americas. Individual employees gained access to perspectives outside their functional background; non-core product-development employees gained assistance with unfamiliar tasks. Cross-functional pairs potentially benefited from more balanced technical and commercial contributions and an increased likelihood of highly rated proposals. Managers could consider smaller or more flexible arrangements when seeking efficiency, while retaining AI-assisted human collaboration when prioritizing outstanding ideas. The authors recommend investing in workers’ AI interaction capabilities and broader cross-functional thinking. These are implications for innovation-focused knowledge work and organizational design, not findings about lawyers, legal clients, legal markets, headcount reductions or public access to services.
